title: Flour types for baking
subtitle: choosing the right flour for bread, cakes, pastry, and biscuits
excerpt: The flour you use changes the texture of everything you bake. Plain flour, self-raising flour, strong bread flour, and wholemeal flour all behave differently because of their protein content, which determines how much gluten can develop. This guide covers the main flour types found in British shops and the baking jobs each one is suited to.
sourceNotes: Flour classification and protein content guidance from standard British flour-milling practice. Protein ranges from standard UK flour packaging.

glossaryTerms.definition: A protein network formed when flour and water are mixed and worked. Higher protein flour develops more gluten, which gives bread its chewy structure. Lower protein flour gives cakes and pastry their tender, crumbly texture.

The proportion of protein in flour, typically shown on the packaging as a percentage of 100 g. It determines how much gluten can develop when the flour is mixed with water. Higher protein = more gluten potential = more structure.

content.text: Flour type is the most important variable in baking. The protein content (shown on the packet) determines how much

can form when the flour is mixed with water. Bread needs high-gluten flour to build a strong, stretchy network. Cakes and pastry need low-gluten flour so they stay tender. Using the wrong flour is one of the most common causes of tough cake and flat bread.
Strong white bread flour (11 to 13% protein)

of the standard range. Use for yeasted breads, pizza dough, and enriched doughs like brioche. The high gluten potential allows the dough to trap carbon dioxide and produce an open, chewy crumb. Do not use for cakes or pastry: the result will be tough.

The most versatile baking flour. Use for pastry, shortbread, biscuits, and as the base for cake recipes that use baking powder as the raising agent. The lower protein content gives a tender, crumbly or short texture. Also used for batters (pancakes, Yorkshire puddings) and as a thickener for sauces.
Self-raising flour (9 to 10% protein, with baking powder added)

Plain flour with baking powder already added (usually at a ratio of 2 teaspoons baking powder per 150 g flour). Use for Victoria sponges, scones, and other cakes where a light lift is needed. Do not substitute for bread flour in bread recipes: there is no gluten development and the baking powder will not replace yeast.

Milled from the whole grain with the bran and germ included. Higher protein than white flour but the bran particles cut gluten strands, giving a denser, heavier loaf. Bread made with 100% wholemeal is noticeably denser than white bread; most recipes use a blend of wholemeal and strong white flour to balance density and structure.
Spelt flour (14 to 16% protein, but fragile gluten)

Spelt has high protein content but the gluten it forms is fragile and extensible rather than strong and elastic. Spelt bread over-kneaded or over-proofed collapses easily. Treat it gently: knead briefly, handle carefully, and watch the proof closely.
Rice flour and other gluten-free flours

Rice flour, oat flour, and buckwheat flour contain no gluten (or only very low levels). Used for gluten-free baking and as a proportion in shortbread for extra crunch. Gluten-free bread requires xanthan gum or psyllium husk to mimic the structure gluten provides.

attrs.problem: Bread made with plain flour is dense and barely rises
attrs.avoid: Avoid using plain flour where a recipe calls for strong bread flour; plain flour lacks the protein for bread gluten.
attrs.fix: Use strong white bread flour (11 to 13% protein) for any yeasted bread recipe.

attrs.problem: Cake is very tough with a bread-like texture
attrs.avoid: Avoid using bread flour for cakes; the high protein content gives a chewy, bread-like crumb.
attrs.fix: Use plain or self-raising flour for cakes to keep the crumb tender.
